DNA replication: Before a cell can divide, it must copy its DNA — all of it, once, accurately. The double helix unzips as helicase breaks the hydrogen bonds between base pairs, and each exposed strand becomes a template. DNA polymerase builds the new strand by matching free nucleotides to the template — A with T, C with G — but it can only build in one direction, so one strand is made continuously and the other in short Okazaki fragments that ligase later seals. The result is semi-conservative: each daughter molecule keeps one original strand and one new one, and proofreading keeps errors near one in a billion bases.
cell structure: Every living thing is built from cells, and every cell runs the same basic plan: a membrane-wrapped interior where organelles divide the work. The nucleus stores the DNA — the instruction set — while ribosomes build proteins from those instructions. Mitochondria release energy from food molecules, the cytoskeleton gives the cell its shape and moves materials around, and the cytoplasm is the gel where most chemistry happens. Plant cells add a rigid wall and chloroplasts; animal cells do without both. Structure is not decoration — each part exists because it does a job the whole cell depends on.
membranes: The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: two sheets of fat-like molecules with their water-loving heads facing out and water-fearing tails facing in. That arrangement makes the membrane selectively permeable — small uncharged molecules slip through, while ions and large molecules need help from embedded proteins. Channel proteins form pores, carrier proteins shuttle specific cargo, and receptor proteins pass signals inward. Cholesterol tucked between the phospholipids keeps the membrane fluid but stable. The membrane is therefore both a wall and a customs post: it decides what enters, what leaves, and what the cell hears about the world outside.
mitosis: Mitosis divides one nucleus into two genetically identical nuclei. In prophase the copied chromosomes condense and the spindle — a scaffold of microtubules — begins to form. Metaphase lines the chromosomes along the cell's equator, each attached to spindle fibers from both poles, a checkpoint that ensures every daughter gets a full set. Anaphase pulls the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles. Telophase wraps each set in a new nuclear envelope, and cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm. One cell in, two identical cells out — the mechanism behind growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.
photosynthesis: Photosynthesis is how plants, algae, and some bacteria turn light energy into stored chemical energy. Inside chloroplasts, pigments — chiefly chlorophyll — absorb mostly blue and red light, which is why leaves look green. In the light-dependent reactions, water is split, releasing oxygen, and its energy is captured in the carriers ATP and NADPH. The Calvin cycle then spends those carriers to build sugars from carbon dioxide, no light required. The balance sheet: carbon dioxide plus water becomes glucose plus oxygen — and nearly every food chain on Earth runs on that captured sunlight.
respiration: Cellular respiration releases the energy photosynthesis stored. It runs in three acts. Glycolysis, in the cytoplasm, splits one glucose into two pyruvate molecules and nets a small payment of ATP — no oxygen needed. The Krebs cycle, in the mitochondrial matrix, strips the pyruvate down to carbon dioxide and loads energy carriers. The electron transport chain then spends those carriers, with oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming water and driving the bulk of ATP production. Total yield: roughly thirty ATP per glucose — the cell's spendable currency, earned by controlled burning instead of fire.
